Krill fisheries in the Southern Ocean have drastically expanded in recent years, with the fisheries’ 620 000 metric tonne catch limit being reached for the first time during the 2024/2025 fishing season1. Such industrial fishing activities, conducted by a growing number of supertrawlers, are causing significant risks for fragile marine ecosystems. Krill are a keystone species in the Southern Ocean food chain and play a critical role in climate change mitigation. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the scientific community and NGOs2 have raised the alarm over this dramatic situation. In November 2025, the session of the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR) concluded with no progress3 on the creation of new marine protected areas, which was vetoed by contracting parties such as China or Russia, or on the renewal of a conservation measure that allocated catches across different areas. Norway has proposed almost doubling the catch limit allowed in the Southern Ocean. Given CCAMLR’s failure to take action to protect Antarctic ecosystems: 1.
What are the Commission and the Member States doing to step up EU action to prevent krill populations from collapsing?
Will the Commission support a moratorium or a closure of krill fisheries in the Southern Ocean to protect Antarctica’s marine ecosystems?

What are the Commission and the Member States doing to step up EU action to prevent krill populations from collapsing?
Will the Commission support a moratorium or a closure of krill fisheries in the Southern Ocean to protect Antarctica’s marine ecosystems?

(29 April 2026) The European Union attaches great importance to the protection of Antarctic krill and to its critical role in the Antarctic ecosystem. The Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR) has generally ensured that the krill fishery in Antarctica remains at sustainable levels (1), in accordance with the precautionary principle and ecosystem approach. Following the lack of agreement during the 43rd CCAMLR annual meeting to retain a catch limit distribution mechanism, catches are increasingly concentrated in specific areas of the Antarctic Peninsula region, thereby negatively affecting these marine ecosystems, including krill-dependent predators such as penguins, seals, and whales. For this reason, the EU has strongly advocated during the 44th CCAMLR annual meeting for the reintroduction, as a matter of urgency, of a distribution of the krill catch limit in the Antarctic Peninsula region on smaller spatial and temporal scales. At the same time the EU promotes improvements to the krill fishery management approach including via regular biomass surveys, better data collection and enhanced ecosystem monitoring. The EU also supports the harmonisation of the revised krill management approach with spatial management measures through proposals to create marine protected areas, which would contribute to safeguarding key krill habitats and foraging grounds.
